title: The Real Reason Monkeys Groom Each Other (+9 More)

intro.say: A woodpecker slams its head into a tree twelve thousand times a day. And it never gets a headache.
A panda that is secretly a meat-eater. A goat whose eyes rotate inside its head. And a cat that is not playing at all.
Here are ten animal mysteries, finally solved. And number one is something you have seen a hundred times, but the real reason has nothing to do with bugs. Stay for it.

chapters.title: Why some white animals aren't albino

scenes.say: Not every white animal is an albino. To tell the difference, you only need to look at one thing: the eyes.
True albinos can't make melanin, the dark pigment in skin, fur and eyes. Their eyes look pink or red, because blood vessels shine right through.
Experts estimate that only about one in ten thousand mammals is born albino. Without melanin, their eyesight is often poor.
Leucistic animals are different. They lose pigment in their fur or feathers, but their eyes stay dark. Some are pure white, others only have white patches.
And the twist: white tigers aren't albino either. Look closely, their stripes are still there, and their eyes are usually blue.
Most people think turkeys can't fly. Wild turkeys can, and they are surprisingly fast.
In short bursts, a wild turkey can hit about fifty five miles per hour. On the ground, it can sprint at around twenty five.
Every evening, a flock flaps up into the treetops to sleep, high above the foxes and coyotes on the ground.
So where does the myth come from? The turkey on your plate is a different bird. Farm turkeys are bred with huge breast muscles and short wings, far too heavy to fly.
In the nineteen thirties, only about thirty thousand wild turkeys were left in America. Today there are around seven million, and every one of them can fly.
Penguins look clumsy when they walk. But that wobbly waddle is actually a clever energy trick.
Short legs make walking expensive. A penguin burns about twice the energy of a dog its size, just to walk the same distance.
So scientists filmed emperor penguins walking. The side to side rock works like a pendulum. Each sway stores energy, then hands it back for the next step.
Penguins got back up to eighty percent of their energy per stride. Humans manage about sixty five.
And those short legs are no mistake. Underwater, they make penguins sleek and fast. Emperor penguins have been recorded diving more than five hundred meters deep.
But the next animal has an even stranger body part. Its pupils are rectangles.
Look a goat in the eye, and you will see a sideways rectangle. That strange shape is a survival tool.
The wide slit gives a panoramic view of the ground around them, perfect for spotting a predator sneaking up. It also blocks dazzling sunlight from above.
In twenty fifteen, scientists at Berkeley compared the pupils of two hundred and fourteen land animals. Of forty two plant-eating prey animals, thirty six had horizontal pupils.
Hunters that ambush their prey, like many cats and snakes, tend to have vertical slits instead. Pupil shape tells you who is the hunter, and who is the hunted.
And here's the weird part. When a goat lowers its head to graze, its eyes roll in their sockets, to keep those pupils level with the horizon.

chapters.title: Why birds puff up in winter

scenes.say: In winter, birds turn into fluffy little balls. That puffy look isn't fat. It's air.
Fluffing up creates hundreds of tiny air pockets between the feathers. Those pockets trap body heat, just like a down jacket.
And birds run hot. Their body temperature is about one hundred and five degrees Fahrenheit, so keeping that heat in is a big deal.
Their bare legs are the weak spot, so many birds tuck one leg up into their feathers. Chickadees even let their feet cool to near freezing, to save energy.
On cold nights, chickadees can even lower their whole body temperature by several degrees, a kind of mini hibernation every single night.
But the next bird has a bigger problem than the cold. It spends all day hitting its head.
A woodpecker can hammer a tree about twelve thousand times a day. So why doesn't it hurt?
For years, people thought its skull worked like a shock absorber. But in twenty twenty two, scientists filmed three species with high-speed cameras.
The head didn't cushion anything. It hit like a stiff hammer. A cushion would soak up the force, and make every peck weaker.
The real trick is size. A woodpecker's brain is tiny, so the forces stay safe. It would have to peck about twice as fast to hurt itself.
And there's a bonus. Its long tongue is so long that, when pulled in, it wraps all the way around the back of its skull.
Horses can sleep standing up, without falling over. Their legs have a built-in lock called the stay apparatus.
Tendons and ligaments hold the joints steady, so the muscles can relax completely. The horse dozes, and its legs do the work.
Why bother? Horses are prey, and getting up off the ground takes time. Standing up, they can bolt the second a predator shows up.
Horses have the largest eyes of any land mammal, set on the sides of the head, so they can see almost all the way around.
But dream sleep only happens lying down, at least about twenty five minutes a day. So while one horse lies down, another stays up as a lookout.
Coming up next: an animal that eats all day long, and still barely gets any food out of it.

chapters.title: Why pandas eat bamboo with a meat-eater's gut

scenes.say: The giant panda is a carnivore. It is a true bear, with a short, simple gut built for meat.
Yet bamboo makes up about ninety nine percent of its diet. And that meat-eater's gut can only digest around seventeen percent of it.
So pandas make up for it with volume. They eat about twelve kilos of bamboo a day, and chew for ten to twelve hours, every single day.
They even have a fake thumb, an extra-long wrist bone, to grip the stalks while they chew.
Pandas switched to bamboo millions of years ago. Their gut never did. They are meat-eaters that live on salad.

chapters.title: Why cats go crazy for laser dots

scenes.say: Your cat isn't playing with that laser dot. It's hunting it.
Cats are built to chase anything small and fast, like a mouse. Their eyes are packed with rod cells, which are super sensitive to motion.
Their ears are tuned for prey too. Cats can hear high squeaks far above what we can hear, the kind of sounds mice and rats make.
So a tiny, darting red dot looks exactly like prey running for cover. It's the same stalk, crouch and pounce you see in lions and leopards.
But there's a catch. The dot can never be caught. With no reward, some cats get frustrated and even start biting or scratching.
So end every laser game on a real toy your cat can grab. Let it finish the hunt.
Monkeys spend hours picking through each other's fur. Most people think they're just eating bugs.
They do remove dirt, dead skin and the odd tick. But that's not the main reason. Grooming is how monkeys make friends.
In a nineteen eighty nine study, feel-good chemicals called endorphins rose by up to one hundred and eighty six percent in monkeys that got to groom a partner.
Being groomed is basically a massage. In rhesus macaques, the heart rate slows down faster while they are being groomed.
And grooming works like money. Chimpanzees are more likely to share food with someone who groomed them earlier that day.
But with too many friends, there aren't enough hours. One scientist argues that's why humans swapped grooming for gossip. So when you chat with a friend, you're kind of grooming them.

outro.say: So which one surprised you most? The goat's rotating eyes, the woodpecker's hammer head, or the monkeys trading grooming for food? Tell us in the comments.
